issues.legal_issue: A time-limited exemption from rent-control legislation for new buildings is constitutionally valid when it reasonably incentivizes construction to address housing scarcity.
material_facts: The amended provision exempted buildings completed on or after the Act’s commencement from rent-control legislation for ten years from completion.
The exemption was intended to encourage new construction, increase the supply of accommodation, and ultimately mitigate tenants’ hardship.
The exemption was for a definite period, which the Court considered neither too long nor unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The exemption was constitutionally valid and was not arbitrary or unreasonable under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit a reasonable, time-limited incentive for new construction where the incentive has a rational connection to easing accommodation scarcity and mitigating tenants’ hardship. The duration and effective date of such an exemption are ordinarily matters of legislative policy, subject to review if unreasonable or arbitrary. The Court relied on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and distinguished Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, which concerned an exemption of indefinite duration.

predicates.a_constitutional_challenge_to_a_rent_con: A party challenged the constitutional validity of an exemption from rent-control protections.
predicates.the_exemption_encourages_new_constructio: The exemption was provided as an incentive to persons who construct new buildings.
predicates.the_exemption_has_a_rational_connection_: The exemption was intended to increase accommodation and thereby address housing scarcity and tenants’ hardship.
predicates.the_exemption_is_for_a_definite_reasonab: The exemption lasts for a defined period that is not unduly long.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a rent-control exemption, the exemption encourages new construction, is connected to reducing housing scarcity, and lasts for a definite reasonable period, the rule treats the exemption as constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: Classifying buildings according to whether their construction was completed before or on or after the commencement of rent-control legislation is constitutionally permissible when the distinction is rationally related to encouraging new construction.
material_facts: The provision exempted buildings completed on or after the Act’s commencement, while buildings completed earlier remained subject to rent-control protections.
The distinction was based on when construction was completed and was intended to encourage construction after the Act commenced.
The Court found that the classification had an intelligible basis and a rational connection to the objective of increasing accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The classification was not arbitrary or invidiously discriminatory and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia and have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied this principle to the classification of buildings and their landlords and tenants by the time of construction, relying on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and finding Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh inapplicable to the time-limited exemption at issue.

predicates.a_challenge_to_building_classification_i: A party challenged a classification of buildings made by a rent-control law.
predicates.buildings_are_classified_by_construction: The law distinguishes buildings according to when their construction was completed in relation to the law’s commencement.
predicates.the_classification_encourages_new_constr: The distinction is intended to encourage the construction of new buildings.
predicates.the_classification_has_a_rational_relati: The distinction is rationally connected to increasing the supply of accommodation.

issues.definition: When a rent-control classification distinguishes buildings by construction timing to encourage new construction and is rationally connected to increasing accommodation, the rule treats the classification as consistent with equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment operates prospectively when it takes effect after enactment, even if it applies to buildings completed before the amendment, and it does not remove a vested tenant right that the earlier law did not confer.
material_facts: The amendment was enacted in 1978 and applied the exemption to buildings completed on or after the Act’s commencement in 1973.
The Court construed the amendment as taking effect after its incorporation into the Act, despite covering buildings completed before the amendment.
The earlier provision had not conferred a vested right on tenants to remain governed by the Act without the amended exemption.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was prospective in operation and did not take away any vested right of the tenants.
issues.legal_principle: A provision is not retrospective merely because its application refers to events predating its enactment, if the provision operates from the time it is incorporated into the law. The Court held that no vested tenant right arose under the earlier provision and stated that a legislature may cure a constitutional defect through a validating enactment, including one with retrospective effect, if it acts within its competence. It relied on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and found Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh inapplicable.

predicates.a_challenge_to_a_rent_control_amendment: A party challenged an amendment to a law regulating rent and eviction.
predicates.the_amendment_takes_effect_after_enactme: The amendment operates after it is incorporated into the law.
predicates.the_amendment_covers_buildings_completed: The amendment’s eligibility criteria include buildings completed before the amendment was enacted.
predicates.the_prior_law_conferred_no_vested_right: The earlier law did not give tenants a vested right to continued application of its provisions.

issues.definition: When a rent-control amendment takes effect after enactment, covers buildings completed earlier, and the prior law conferred no vested right, the rule treats the amendment as prospective and as not removing a vested right.
